name: Reflex
line: Reflex builds fast recall of basic facts in games. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Reflex: Reflex builds fast recall of basic facts in games. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Reflex builds fast, accurate recall of the basic facts of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, in games that follow a quick fluency check at the start of each session [1]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous across all of math. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. Every answer updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Each Reflex session begins with a quick fluency check and just-in-time coaching, and practice in games follows [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Reflex the unit is the basic fact. Facts are grouped in fact families and practiced in games after brief coaching [1][3]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [10].

reasons.title: What counts as learned
reasons.body: In AMP an answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. A skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. In Reflex the goal is fluency: fast, accurate recall. Its games ask for faster answers as a learner improves [1].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP runs from counting through precalculus in one program, on one map of skills, and keeps a separate level for each part of math. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Reflex practices the basic facts of the four operations, for grade 2 and up [1][2].

rows.range: Basic facts of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, grade 2 and up [1][2].

rows.next: The program picks which facts to practice, by fact family [1].
rows.mastery: Fluency: fast, accurate recall. Games ask for faster answers as a learner improves [1].

rows.print: None found in the pages we read [1][2].
rows.evidence: Two studies in a national intervention chart, with effects on targeted measures [5]. No Evidence for ESSA rating [6][7].

theirs: Reflex comes from ExploreLearning. It builds fluency with the basic facts of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, for grade 2 and up [1][2]. ExploreLearning says it delivers "the right facts at the right time" [1].

Each session begins with a quick fluency check and just-in-time coaching [1]. The learner then practices in games that ask for faster answers as recall grows [1]. Practice is built on fact families, the links between related facts [1][3]. Learners earn tokens and certificates as they go [1][2].
credit: Fast, accurate recall of the basic facts is its whole job. The What Works Clearinghouse rates regular timed fluency activities as strong evidence for elementary students who struggle in math [9].
Practice is built on fact families, the links between related facts [1][3].
Two studies in a national chart of intervention tools show significant effects on targeted measures [5].

theirs: The National Center on Intensive Intervention lists two Reflex studies in its academic intervention tools chart. Both are group designs with statistically significant effects on targeted measures. It rates the design of Rudel (2016) convincing, with an effect of 0.84, and Sarrell (2014) partially convincing, with 0.58 [5].

ExploreLearning's featured study comes from one Florida district. Students who used Reflex and Frax, its fractions program, gained more on the i-Ready Diagnostic than students who did not. They were 60% more likely to meet typical growth goals and twice as likely to meet stretch goals [4]. The Reflex site says ExploreLearning conducted it [2]. It compares users with non-users, and the pages we read give no sample size, hours of use or effect size. ExploreLearning labels it ESSA Tier 2 [4].

Evidence for ESSA lists Reflex twice, as Reflex Math and as ExploreLearning Reflex. Both pages say "No studies met inclusion requirements" [6][7]. The What Works Clearinghouse has no intervention report for Reflex [8]. We found no randomized trial of Reflex.
ours: The finding that bears most on this comparison: a meta-analysis of 55 studies found that worked examples improve mathematics performance, with an average effect of g = 0.48 [10]. AMP applies this at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: Your child understands what the operations mean and needs fast, automatic recall of the basic facts.
amp: You want one program from counting through precalculus, with a level for each part of math.
You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice, mixed with other math.
You want printable workbooks made from your child's own record.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Reflex?
questions.answer: Reflex builds fast recall of the basic facts of the four operations, in games that follow a quick fluency check at the start of each session [1]. AMP covers counting through precalculus. Every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Reflex work?
questions.answer: Two Reflex studies in the National Center on Intensive Intervention's chart show statistically significant effects on targeted measures [5]. Evidence for ESSA lists Reflex without a rating [6][7]. We found no randomized trial.

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
